sections.h2: Does Maine have a separate capital gains tax on a house sale?
sections.html:
No. Maine does not publish a separate capital gains rate for home sales. Under 36 M.R.S. §5121, a resident's Maine taxable income starts with federal adjusted gross income, so a taxable gain on your house is carried into the Maine return and taxed on the regular graduated schedule.

That means two questions decide what you owe on a Maine house sale. First, how much of the gain does the federal home sale exclusion remove? Second, where does what is left land on the Maine rate schedule for your filing status?

Both answers depend on facts the sale price alone does not show: how long you lived in the house, what you paid for it, what you spent on improvements, and whether you live in Maine now. This page walks through each piece so you can estimate the bill before you sign anything.

sections.h2: How much of the gain can a Maine homeowner exclude?
sections.html:
Most owners who lived in the house can exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or up to $500,000 on a joint return. The IRS describes this in Topic 701, and because the excluded gain never reaches federal adjusted gross income, it does not reach the Maine return either.

TestWhat the IRS says
OwnershipYou or your spouse owned the home at least 24 months of the 5 years before the sale
Use as main homeYou and your spouse each used it as a main residence at least 24 months of those 5 years
Exclusion limitUp to $250,000, or $500,000 if filing jointly
FrequencyGenerally not available if you excluded gain on another home sale within the 2 years before this sale
ReportingA Form 1099-S must be reported even if all the gain is excludable; Form 8949 and Schedule D are used if some gain is not excludable

The two-year ownership and use periods can fall in different stretches, as long as both are met inside the five-year window that ends on the sale date. Partial exclusions and depreciation are handled in IRS Publication 523, which Topic 701 points to.

sections.h2: What are Maine's income tax rates on the gain you cannot exclude?
sections.html:
For 2026 Maine uses three brackets: 5.8 percent, 6.75 percent and 7.15 percent. The thresholds below come from the 2026 Maine Revenue Services rate schedule.

Filing status5.8% applies below6.75% bracket7.15% applies at or above
Single or married filing separately$27,400$27,400 to $64,850$64,850
Head of household$41,100$41,100 to $97,300$97,300
Married filing jointly$54,850$54,850 to $129,750$129,750

Starting with tax years beginning in 2026, a 2 percent surcharge applies to Maine taxable income above $1,000,000 for a single filer, $750,000 for married filing separately, and $1,500,000 for married filing jointly or head of household. A large gain from a high-value house or a multi-parcel sale can reach that level.

The same schedule lists a 2026 standard deduction of $15,700 for a single filer and $31,400 for a joint return, plus a $5,300 personal exemption per taxpayer.

sections.h2: What federal rate applies to a taxable house gain?
sections.html:
A house you owned for more than one year produces a long-term gain, taxed federally at 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on income. The IRS explains the holding period and rates in Topic 409.

  • For taxable years beginning in 2025, the 0 percent rate applies at or below $48,350 (single), $96,700 (married filing jointly) or $64,750 (head of household).
  • The 15 percent rate runs up to $533,400 (single), $600,050 (married filing jointly) or $566,700 (head of household).
  • Above those amounts the rate is 20 percent.
  • Gain on a house held one year or less is short-term and taxed as ordinary income.
  • The portion of gain from real property that is unrecaptured section 1250 gain is taxed at a maximum 25 percent.

The Maine bill is added on top of the federal one. Someone with a $90,000 taxable gain owes Maine tax at the Maine brackets above, no matter which federal rate applies.

sections.h2: What happens if you live outside Maine and sell a Maine house?
sections.html:
The buyer or closing agent must withhold 2.5 percent of the sale price when the seller is a nonresident and the price is $100,000 or more. Maine Revenue Services' real estate withholding FAQ says this applies to nonresident individuals, estates and businesses.

  • The withholding is an estimated payment toward Maine tax on the gain. It is not the final tax.
  • With several owners, the buyer withholds 2.5 percent of each nonresident seller's share.
  • The buyer or escrow person files Form REW-1 and pays within 30 days of closing.
  • A Maine resident who does not hand over a signed residency affidavit (Form REW-2 or REW-3) is treated as a nonresident for this purpose.
  • A partnership counts as a Maine resident if at least 75 percent of its ownership is held by Maine residents on the transfer date.

Heirs who live out of state and inherit a Maine house are often surprised here. An estate selling Maine property is within the withholding rule too, so the closing agent will ask for a residency affidavit or an exemption certificate.

sections.h2: How can a seller reduce or avoid the 2.5 percent withholding?
sections.html:
File Form REW-5 with Maine Revenue Services before closing. The state says a seller cannot obtain an exemption or reduction after closing, and it asks for at least 5 business days to respond.

  • A full exemption may be available if there is no gain, or if a federal exclusion of gain on a principal residence applies. The state's page does not list a principal residence as a standalone exemption, so the request goes through REW-5.
  • A reduction is possible when your maximum Maine tax on the gain is below 2.5 percent of the sale price. The state calculates it as 7.15 percent of the gain, plus 2 percent of the gain above $1,000,000 (single), $1,500,000 (head of household or married filing jointly) or $750,000 (married filing separately) for tax year 2026.
  • Estates and trusts use 7.15 percent plus 2 percent of gain above $1,000,000. Corporations use 8.93 percent.
  • A like-kind exchange under IRC §1031 still triggers withholding, but you can ask for an exemption with REW-5 and a copy of the exchange contract.
  • Installment sales may qualify for a reduction based on first-year gain.

Consideration under $100,000 avoids withholding, but the state notes that federally taxable gains are still taxable in Maine regardless of the amount. A nonresident seller should expect to file a Maine income tax return for the year of the sale to claim any refund of excess withholding. Refund claims are generally due within three years of the return due date or three years from payment, whichever is later.

sections.h2: How does an inherited house change the numbers?
sections.html:
An heir's starting point is usually the house's value on the date of death, not what the owner paid. IRS Publication 551 lists fair market value at death, the alternate valuation date if the estate elects it, and special-use valuation for qualifying farm or business property.

If the estate had to file a federal Form 706, beneficiaries usually receive a Schedule A (Form 8971), and certain beneficiaries must use the reported value as their basis. One exception: if you or your spouse gave the property to the decedent within one year before death, your basis is the decedent's adjusted basis rather than the date-of-death value.

For a Maine family, this often means a house inherited and sold within a year or two shows little or no gain. The estate-side issues, including Maine's own estate tax lien, are covered on ourx. Basis is generally what you paid, plus improvements that add value, minus allowable depreciation, as the IRS describes in Topic 703.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale fit with Maine tax planning?
sections.html:
A cash sale does not change the tax rules, but it makes the closing date predictable, which helps you plan. You know when the gain is realized, when any withholding is due, and which tax year it belongs to. If you are a nonresident, you can also raise the REW-5 request early, because a seller cannot get an exemption or reduction after closing.

Sellers in Maine often come to us because of an inherited house, a rental with tenants or deferred repairs. Each of those has its own tax angle: basis for heirs, depreciation for landlords, and withholding for owners who moved away. Talk to a licensed tax professional about your own numbers. We can give you a straightforward offer and let your closing agent and accountant handle the filings.

faqs.q: Does Maine tax the profit when I sell my house?
faqs.a: Yes, if the gain is taxable. A resident's Maine income starts from federal adjusted gross income, so any gain not excluded under the federal home sale rules is taxed at Maine's graduated rates. For 2026 those rates are 5.8, 6.75 and 7.15 percent.

faqs.q: How much of my gain can I exclude when selling my Maine home?
faqs.a: Up to $250,000, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the house as your main home for at least 24 months of the last 5 years. You generally cannot use it if you excluded gain on another home within the prior 2 years.

faqs.q: What is Maine real estate withholding?
faqs.a: It is a 2.5 percent withholding on the sale price when a nonresident sells Maine property for $100,000 or more. The buyer or closing agent files Form REW-1 and pays within 30 days of closing. It is only an estimate of the seller's Maine tax.

faqs.q: Can I get the withholding waived?
faqs.a: Possibly. File Form REW-5 with Maine Revenue Services before closing. Exemptions or reductions are available in cases such as no gain, a federal principal residence exclusion, or when your maximum Maine tax is below 2.5 percent of the price. It cannot be requested after closing.

faqs.q: Do heirs owe Maine tax on an inherited house they sell?
faqs.a: Only on gain above their basis. Inherited property generally takes its fair market value at the date of death as basis, so a sale soon after inheritance often shows little gain. A nonresident heir may still face withholding at closing.

faqs.q: Is there a surcharge on large gains in Maine?
faqs.a: Yes, for tax years beginning in 2026. A 2 percent surcharge applies to Maine taxable income above $1,000,000 for single filers, $750,000 for married filing separately, and $1,500,000 for joint filers and heads of household.
